verses.text: Now these are the names of the sons of Israel, who came into Egypt (every man and his household came with Jacob):
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All the souls who came out of Jacob’s body were seventy souls, and Joseph was in Egypt already.
Joseph died, as did all his brothers, and all that generation.
The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who didn’t know Joseph.
He said to his people, “Behold,  the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we.
Come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it happen that when any war breaks out, they also join themselves to our enemies, and fight against us, and escape out of the land.”
Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens. They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Raamses.
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they spread out. They were grieved because of the children of Israel.
The Egyptians ruthlessly made the children of Israel serve,
and they made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and in brick, and in all kinds of service in the field, all their service, in which they ruthlessly made them serve.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, of whom the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah,
and he said, “When you perform the duty of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them on the birth stool; if it is a son, then you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.”
But the midwives feared God,  and didn’t do what the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the baby boys alive.
The king of Egypt called for the midwives, and said to them, “Why have you done this thing, and have saved the boys alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “Because the Hebrew women aren’t like the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous, and give birth before the midwife comes to them.”
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied, and grew very mighty.
Because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “You shall cast every son who is born into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”

footnotes.content: The roll call opens—these seventy souls, named one by one, carried a promise wrapped in their very bones. Every name matters to the God who holds them all. Jacob brought them into Egypt like seeds into dark soil, but they didn't know yet they were meant to grow into a nation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah—the eldest four, foundation stones of what would become God's covenant people. Judah carries a particular weight here; in time, kings and the Messiah would come through his line. The Lord was building His family already.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Issachar, Zebulun, Benjamin—more sons, more tribes yet to be called. In a future desert, they would each receive their portion of promise. The Lord knew them by name before they crossed the border into Egypt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher—the roster completes. Twelve sons, twelve tribes, twelve witnesses to God's faithfulness. Each name represented a family, a dream, a future stake in land not yet possessed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy souls—a small band in a foreign land, and Joseph already gone from them. Yet the Lord counts each one, and from this handful, a multitude will grow. Small seeds often yield the greatest harvests; the Lord delights in that math.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Joseph died, an entire generation passed with him—those who had walked with Jacob, who had seen the covenant promises spoken face to face. Silence came. But God's promises don't die; they wait, patient and sure, for the next generation to wake up and see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like grain multiplying in a field, the children of Israel filled the land. The Lord's word was doing what He promised—fruitfulness even in a foreign soil. Their growth was itself a sign: God's covenant didn't die with Joseph; it was alive and working.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A new pharaoh, ignorant of Joseph and all he had been to Egypt—and in that forgetfulness lay the seed of Israel's bondage. How quickly kingdoms lose their memory. But God remembers. He never forgets His people, no matter how many pharaohs rise and fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear spoke through Pharaoh's words. A ruler watching a people grow more numerous and stronger saw only threat, not blessing. Fear makes us cruel. But the Lord was stirring among those very slaves—He would become their deliverer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh plotted 'wisdom,' but his cleverness was nothing but the scheming of a frightened man. He wanted to bind a people the Lord was calling to freedom. Human strategy against God's purpose always ends the same way—in ash.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Taskmasters, burdens, Pithom and Raamses—cities built on forced labor, monuments to cruelty. Yet the Lord watches what is done in darkness. Every brick laid under the whip matters to Him; every tear matters. This is where the slaves began to cry out, and God heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The harder Pharaoh pressed, the more Israel multiplied. That paradox would have undone him if he'd seen it—God's people cannot be crushed into nothing. Their very bones were fertile with promise. The Egyptians grew grieved, and still the covenant stood firm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ruthlessness—the word sits heavy here. But I've learned that those moments when the world seems most cruel are often when God is most at work, hidden and patient. The slaves didn't yet know a deliverer was coming. We often don't, either, until He arrives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mortar and brick, labor in field and house—every sort of service, relentless and bitter. The text names it honestly. God honors that honesty; He sees servitude and remembers those who endure it. Their suffering wouldn't be wasted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shiphrah and Puah—midwives named, remembered, their courage inscribed. How often the Lord lifts up the small and hidden ones, the women no powerful court would notice. These two would become heroes of faith, their names outlasting Pharaoh's own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An evil command spoke through the king's lips—murder of the innocent, ordered as if it were duty. The midwives heard a choice that night. Some powers demand our obedience; only God deserves that deep allegiance. They would soon learn what courage costs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They feared God more than they feared Pharaoh. In that one choice—to let the baby boys live—Shiphrah and Puah became instruments of grace. The Lord honors those who choose His side, even when the cost is terrifying and the night is long.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's anger rose, and the midwives had to face him. Standing before a king's wrath with only truth and a quiet conscience—that's a different kind of strength than swords. They had already decided what mattered more.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their answer was clever and true—Hebrew women are vigorous, they bear quickly, and the midwives' excuse stands on the truth of nature itself. Wisdom and honesty served them; they didn't need a lie. God watched and approved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God dealt well with the midwives—reward for those who honor Him. Israel multiplied still, and Pharaoh's schemes crumbled. The Lord has a way of turning human wickedness into the very means of His people's growth and blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because they feared God, He gave them families. Shiphrah and Puah, saving lives, were themselves blessed with descendants. The Lord doesn't forget those who stand for the helpless, even when no one watches but Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this desperate command: a tyrant trying to drown the very hope he fears most. Yet infants hidden in baskets, mothers risking everything—these scenes repeat across history when oppression rises. But so does rescue. The pattern holds: grace finds the hidden child.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
